title: Oscillators
intro: An oscillator turns DC power into a periodic signal with no input. In CMOS it is almost always a ring of delay stages or an LC tank with an active circuit that cancels the tank loss, and in practice it is voltage-controlled so a PLL can steer it (Razavi, Chapter 15).

blocks.text: Put an amplifier $H(s)$ in a negative-feedback loop. The closed-loop gain is $H/(1+H)$; if at some frequency $\omega_0$ the loop gain equals $-1$, this gain is infinite and the circuit amplifies its own noise at $\omega_0$ without bound. Followed around the loop, a noise component returns with gain $|H|$ each trip: the amplitude forms the series $V_0(1 + |H| + |H|^2 + \dots)$, which converges to $V_0/(1-|H|)$ for $|H|<1$ and grows for $|H| \ge 1$.

blocks.alt: Block diagram: a noise source enters a summing node, passes through an amplifier H(s) to the output, and the output is fed back to the minus input of the summing node.
blocks.caption: The feedback view: an oscillator is a loop whose gain reaches minus one at one frequency.

blocks.text: The 180° here is phase that $H$ itself adds, on top of the 180° the subtractor already contributes; together they make 360° and the returning signal reinforces the original. A loop can get that phase in three equivalent ways: an inverting amplifier with 180° of frequency-dependent shift, a non-inverting amplifier with 360° in its stages, or a non-inverting one with 0° at $\omega_0$ (an LC loop at resonance). Because process and temperature move the gain, designs aim for a small-signal loop gain two to three times the minimum.

Once the oscillation grows, the stages saturate. The gain averaged over a cycle falls until it is exactly one, which is what sets the amplitude: the poles start in the right half plane and are pushed back onto the $j\omega$ axis by nonlinearity.

items: Ring oscillators: three or more inverting stages in a loop. Small, wide tuning range, many phases for free, but noisy and supply-sensitive.

LC oscillators: a resonant tank whose loss is cancelled by a cross-coupled pair (negative-Gm) or a single-transistor Colpitts circuit. Much lower phase noise and higher frequencies, but they need inductors (area) and tune over a narrow range.
Ring Oscillators: why three stages, the minimum gain and frequency, large-signal delay, differential rings and loads.
LC Tanks and Tuned Stages: resonance, Q, series-to-parallel conversion, tuned amplifiers.
Cross-Coupled LC Oscillators: the negative-Gm oscillator, start-up, amplitude, supply sensitivity.
Colpitts and One-Port Oscillators: the capacitive-divider oscillator and the negative-resistance view.
VCOs and Ring Tuning: VCO figures of merit and ways to tune a ring.
Varactors and LC Tuning: pn-junction and MOS varactors, tuning range and its limits.
Mathematical Model of VCOs: phase as the integral of frequency, $K_{VCO}/s$, sidebands.

blocks.text: Rule of thumb from the book's opening joke: in high-frequency design, amplifiers oscillate and oscillators don't. An amplifier with too much phase shift and an oscillator with too little gain are the same mistake seen from two sides.

blocks.title: Sub-unity loop gain
blocks.text: A loop has 180° of extra phase at $\omega_0$ but $|H(j\omega_0)| = 0.8$. A noise burst of amplitude $V_0$ at $\omega_0$ is injected. What amplitude does the summing node settle to? Does it oscillate?
solution: The returning copies add in phase: $V_0(1 + 0.8 + 0.8^2 + \dots) = V_0/(1 - 0.8) = 5V_0$.
The sum converges, so the response decays once the burst ends; the circuit rings but does not sustain oscillation.
blocks.answer: Settles at $5V_0$ while driven; no oscillation.

blocks.title: Gain margin for start-up
blocks.text: An oscillator's loop gain is nominally 2.5 at the oscillation frequency. Over corners the transconductance can fall by 35% and the tank resistance by 20%. Does it still start?
solution: The loop gain scales with $g_m R$: $2.5 \times 0.65 \times 0.8 = 1.3$.
This is still above 1, so it starts in the worst corner, though with little margin.
